card.quiz: Largest axillary branch. Splits into the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries.

parts.label: Subscapular vein
parts.group: Systemic veins.g > Right subclavian vein > Axillary vein.r

card.name: Subscapular vein
card.summary: A vein that collects blood from the back of the shoulder blade region. It follows the subscapular artery.
card.into: Axillary vein
card.course: It runs with the subscapular artery along the lateral border of subscapularis and empties into the axillary vein.
card.clinical: It is a deep tributary that surgeons may meet during axillary lymph node surgery.
card.quiz: Accompanies the largest axillary artery branch on the back wall of the armpit.

parts.label: Superficial palmar arch
parts.group: Axillary artery.r > Brachial artery.r > Ulnar artery.r

card.name: Superficial palmar arch
card.summary: An arterial arch in the palm. The ulnar artery forms most of it.
card.from: Ulnar artery (completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery or another branch)
card.course: It crosses the palm under the palmar aponeurosis and over the long flexor tendons. It lies roughly level with the distal border of the fully extended thumb.
branches: Proper palmar digital artery to the little finger
card.clinical: It can be cut by deep palm lacerations and heavy bleeding may follow. The Allen test checks whether the arches are complete.
card.quiz: Mainly the ulnar artery. Lies superficial to the long flexor tendons.

parts.label: Superficial venous palmar arch
parts.group: Axillary vein.r > Brachial veins.r > Ulnar veins.r

card.name: Superficial venous palmar arch
card.summary: A pair of veins that accompany the superficial palmar arterial arch.
card.into: Ulnar veins
card.course: It lies in the palm beside the superficial palmar arterial arch and drains mostly toward the ulnar side of the forearm.
card.clinical: It lies below the palmar aponeurosis, so it is at risk in deep cuts of the palm.
card.quiz: Veins that accompany the ulnar-side arterial arch of the palm.

parts.label: Superior ulnar collateral artery
parts.group: Right subclavian artery > Axillary artery.r > Brachial artery.r

card.name: Superior ulnar collateral artery
card.summary: A branch of the brachial artery that runs with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
card.from: Brachial artery (near the middle of the arm)
card.course: It pierces the medial intermuscular septum with the ulnar nerve. It passes behind the medial epicondyle and meets the posterior ulnar recurrent artery.
card.clinical: It lies next to the ulnar nerve. Surgeons protect it during ulnar nerve transposition at the elbow.
card.quiz: Runs with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.

parts.label: Suprascapular artery
parts.group: Systemic arteries.g > Right subclavian artery > Thyrocervical trunk.r

card.name: Suprascapular artery
card.summary: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk that supplies the muscles on the back of the scapula.
card.from: Thyrocervical trunk (first part of the subclavian artery)
card.course: It runs across the root of the neck and passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament. The suprascapular nerve passes under it.
card.clinical: Memory aid: the artery goes over the ligament and the nerve goes under. It meets the circumflex scapular artery.
card.quiz: Passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament. The nerve goes under.

parts.label: Suprascapular vein
parts.group: Systemic veins.g > Right subclavian vein > External jugular vein.r

card.name: Suprascapular vein
card.summary: A vein that follows the suprascapular artery and drains the back of the scapula.
card.into: External jugular vein (sometimes the subclavian vein)
card.course: It accompanies the suprascapular artery across the top of the scapula and drains into the external jugular vein in the neck.
card.clinical: It lies in the lower neck behind the clavicle, so it can be injured in clavicle fractures or neck surgery.
card.quiz: Follows the artery that passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament. Ends in the external jugular vein.

parts.label: Thoraco-acromial artery
parts.group: Systemic arteries.g > Right subclavian artery > Axillary artery.r

card.name: Thoraco-acromial artery
card.summary: A short, wide branch of the axillary artery. It pierces the clavipectoral fascia and splits into four branches.
card.from: Axillary artery (second part, behind pectoralis minor)
card.course: It emerges at the upper border of pectoralis minor, pierces the clavipectoral membrane, and divides at once into its branches.
card.clinical: It is a landmark vessel in the deltopectoral approach. It can bleed when surgeons release the clavipectoral fascia.
card.quiz: Pierces the clavipectoral fascia, then splits into pectoral, deltoid, acromial, and clavicular branches.

parts.label: Thoracodorsal artery
parts.group: Right subclavian artery > Axillary artery.r > Subscapular artery.r

card.name: Thoracodorsal artery
card.summary: The continuation of the subscapular artery. It travels with the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi.
card.from: Subscapular artery (its continuation)
card.course: It runs down the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal nerve and enters the deep surface of latissimus dorsi.
card.clinical: Surgeons use it as the pedicle of the latissimus dorsi flap for breast reconstruction.
card.quiz: Continuation of the subscapular artery that runs down the posterior axillary wall to latissimus dorsi.

parts.label: Thoracodorsal vein
parts.group: Systemic veins.g > Right subclavian vein > Axillary vein.r

card.name: Thoracodorsal vein
card.summary: A vein that drains latissimus dorsi. It runs with the thoracodorsal artery and nerve.
card.into: Subscapular vein (or directly into the axillary vein)
card.course: It runs up the posterior axillary wall beside the thoracodorsal artery and nerve.
card.clinical: Surgeons use it with its artery as the vascular pedicle of a latissimus dorsi flap.
card.quiz: Drains latissimus dorsi and runs up the posterior axillary wall with its artery and nerve.

parts.label: Ulnar artery
parts.group: Right subclavian artery > Axillary artery.r > Brachial artery.r

card.name: Ulnar artery
card.summary: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery. It runs along the little finger side of the forearm.
card.from: Brachial artery (in the cubital fossa)
card.course: It passes deep to pronator teres and runs between flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis. At the wrist it lies beside the ulnar nerve and continues as the superficial palmar arch.
branches: Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries
supplies: Deep forearm muscles (via the interosseous arteries)
Palm and little finger side of the hand
card.clinical: A fracture of the hook of the hamate or a cut at the wrist can injure it with the ulnar nerve. The Allen test uses it.
card.quiz: Larger terminal branch of the brachial artery. Becomes the superficial palmar arch.

parts.label: Ulnar recurrent artery
parts.group: Axillary artery.r > Brachial artery.r > Ulnar artery.r

card.name: Ulnar recurrent arteries
card.summary: Small branches of the ulnar artery that turn back up toward the elbow. They have anterior and posterior parts.
card.from: Ulnar artery (just below the elbow)
card.course: The anterior branch runs up in front of the medial epicondyle. The posterior branch runs up behind it, near the ulnar nerve.
card.clinical: They join the collateral arteries to form the elbow anastomosis, which supplies the joint and protects blood flow.
card.quiz: Turn back from the main medial forearm artery toward the medial epicondyle.

parts.label: Ulnar veins
parts.group: Right subclavian vein > Axillary vein.r > Brachial veins.r

card.name: Ulnar veins
card.summary: A pair of deep veins that accompany the ulnar artery.
drains: Deep structures of the medial forearm
card.into: Brachial veins (after joining the radial veins)
card.course: They start from the superficial venous palmar arch, run up the medial forearm beside the ulnar artery, and unite with the radial veins.
card.clinical: They run with the ulnar artery, so a deep forearm wound on the medial side can injure the artery and its veins together.
card.quiz: Paired deep veins on the little-finger side of the forearm that start from the superficial venous palmar arch.

glossary.def: Moving a limb away from the midline of the body. For the fingers, away from the middle finger.
Moving a limb toward the midline of the body. For the fingers, toward the middle finger.
A connection between two vessels, which gives blood a second route to an area.
Toward the front of the body.
A broad, flat sheet of tendon that attaches a muscle to bone or to another muscle.
A joint, or the place where two bones meet.
A smaller nerve or vessel that leaves a larger one.
A circular movement that combines flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in turn.
A group of muscles, with their nerve and blood supply, held together by fascia.
A rounded knob at the end of a bone that forms part of a joint.
In the brachial plexus, one of three bundles (lateral, posterior, medial) named for their position around the axillary artery.
Farther from the surface of the body.
Lowering a body part downward, such as pulling the shoulders down.
An area of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve.
Farther from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.
Relating to the back of the hand, or the back surface of a structure.
Lifting a body part upward, such as shrugging the shoulders.
A bump on the side of a bone above a joint surface, where muscles and ligaments attach.
The end of a long bone, which grows from its own center of ossification.
A movement that increases the angle at a joint, such as straightening the elbow.
A sheet of connective tissue that wraps muscles and other structures.
A movement that decreases the angle at a joint, such as bending the elbow.
A hole in a bone through which nerves or vessels pass.
A shallow hollow or depression on a bone.
The nerve supply to a muscle, organ or area of skin.
The attachment of a muscle that usually moves when the muscle contracts, usually farther from the trunk.
Farther from the midline of the body. In the anatomical position, the thumb side of the forearm is lateral.
Turning the front of a limb away from the midline, around its long axis.
A tough band of connective tissue that joins one bone to another.
Closer to the midline of the body. In the anatomical position, the little-finger side of the forearm is medial.
Turning the front of a limb toward the midline, around its long axis.
Bringing the tip of the thumb across the palm to touch another fingertip.
The attachment of a muscle that stays fixed, usually closer to the trunk, when the muscle contracts.
The process of forming bone, usually from cartilage or membrane.
Relating to the palm side of the hand, the same as anterior in the hand.
A network of nerves or vessels that join and then split again.
Toward the back of the body.
A bony projection that sticks out from a bone.
Turning the forearm so the palm faces backward or down.
Moving the scapula forward around the rib cage, away from the spine.
Closer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.
A thick band of fascia that holds tendons close to a joint, such as at the wrist.
Moving the scapula backward toward the spine, as when squeezing the shoulder blades together.
In the brachial plexus, one of the five ventral rami (C5 to T1) that form the plexus. These are not the same as the dorsal and ventral roots attached to the spinal cord.
A small bone that develops inside a tendon, such as the pisiform or kneecap.
A groove on a bone, often where a tendon or nerve runs.
Closer to the surface of the body.
Turning the forearm so the palm faces forward or up.
A tough cord of connective tissue that joins a muscle to a bone.
In the brachial plexus, one of three large nerve bundles (upper, middle, lower) formed from the roots.
A small, rounded bump on a bone, often where a tendon attaches.
A large, rough bump on a bone where a muscle or ligament attaches.
Turning the scapula so the socket faces up, which is needed to raise the arm overhead.
